payload.explanation_text: A cell membrane is a thin barrier that surrounds the cell and controls what goes in and out. Its main building blocks are phospholipids. Each phospholipid is amphipathic, meaning it has two different parts: a water-loving head and water-avoiding tails. In water, phospholipids arrange themselves into a bilayer, a double layer in which the heads face outward toward the water on both sides and the tails face inward, away from the water, forming the middle of the membrane. The tails are fatty acid chains. A saturated fatty acid has no double bonds, so its tails are straight and pack tightly together. An unsaturated fatty acid has one or more double bonds, and these create kinks in the tail. Because kinked tails cannot pack as tightly, unsaturated tails make the membrane more fluid. Membrane fluidity, meaning how freely molecules can move, depends on three main factors: the saturation and chain length of the fatty acids, the temperature, and cholesterol. Cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer. When the membrane is very fluid, cholesterol restricts motion and makes it less fluid. When the membrane is cold, cholesterol keeps it from stiffening too much, which widens the range of temperatures over which the membrane stays usable. The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a mosaic of lipids, cholesterol, and proteins, and these components can move sideways within the layer. Singer and Nicolson proposed this model in 1972. The two layers of the membrane, called leaflets, are not identical. Their composition differs, which is called membrane asymmetry. Lipids rarely flip from one leaflet to the other on their own. When flipping does happen, it is usually helped by enzymes called flippases, floppases, and scramblases. Finally, sugars on the outer surface of the membrane form the glycocalyx. These sugars help cells recognize each other and tell self from non-self.

payload.explanation_text:
Fluidity means how easily the molecules in a cell membrane can move around. Membranes are not solid, and two factors help control how fluid they are: the type of fatty acid tails the membrane contains, and cholesterol.

Concept 1: Saturated vs. unsaturated fatty acids. The key clue is the double bond. Saturated tails have no double bonds, so they are straight and pack tightly together, which makes the membrane less fluid. Unsaturated tails do have double bonds, and each double bond creates a kink, or bend, in the tail. Because kinked tails cannot pack as tightly, there is more space between them, so the membrane is more fluid. A simple way to remember it: unsaturated means kinks (double bonds), kinks mean more fluid. Saturated means straight, tight packing, less fluid.

Concept 2: Cholesterol as a fluidity buffer. A buffer keeps something within a workable range. Cholesterol does this for membrane fluidity. When the membrane is very fluid, cholesterol restricts motion, so the membrane does not become too loose. When the membrane is cold, cholesterol keeps it from stiffening too much. Together these two effects widen the temperature range over which the membrane stays in a healthy, flexible state.

payload.explanation_text: Let's look at two ideas that help explain how a cell membrane stays flexible. First, think of the membrane as a sheet made mostly of phospholipids, which have fatty acid tails. Each tail is a chain of carbon atoms, and the way those chains are built changes how the membrane behaves. Saturated fatty acids have straight tails with no double bonds between carbons. Because they are straight, they pack tightly together, which makes the membrane less fluid, meaning less able to flow and move. Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds in their tails. Each double bond creates a kink, or bend, in the tail. These kinks keep the tails from packing tightly, so the membrane stays more fluid. Second, cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer. A buffer is something that keeps a system steady when conditions change. When the membrane is very fluid, cholesterol restricts the motion of the phospholipids, which keeps the membrane from becoming too loose. When the membrane gets cold, cholesterol keeps it from stiffening as much as it otherwise would. This means cholesterol helps the membrane stay usable across a wider range of temperatures, which is what it means to widen the transition range. Together, fatty acid structure and cholesterol help the membrane keep a balanced level of fluidity.
